It builds on [3D Trilinear Interpolation](2613-3d-trilinear-interpolation.md) by modifying the interpolation weights rather than the data structure or lookup count [S1, unofficial][S2].

The claim states that the technique builds on 3D Trilinear Interpolation by modifying interpolation weights rather than the data structure or lookup count. Source [S1] explicitly states: 'we recommend applying the smoothstep function... to the d-linear interpolation weights.' It contrasts this with higher-order interpolation (biquadratic/bicubic) which requires looking up more vertices (3 or 4 instead of 2), implying the proposed method keeps the lookup count standard (2 vertices per dimension, consistent with trilinear). Furthermore, Source [S2] notes that the NGLOD implementation differs in the underlying data structure, whereas the smooth interpolation method described is applied to the hash encoding (which uses a hash table), implying the data structure itself remains a hash table (standard for the base method) while only the weights are modified. Thus, all facts in the claim are supported by the evidence.

*   **Input:** A query point $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ and a multiresolution hash encoding structure with $L$ resolution levels [S1, unofficial][S2].

The claim accurately reflects the technical details provided in both Source [S1] and Source [S2]. Specifically: 1) The sources confirm that multiresolution hash encoding uses trilinear interpolation by default. 2) They describe applying the smoothstep function $s_1(x) = x^2(3-2x)$ to the interpolation weights to achieve C1-smoothness. 3) They note that the derivative $S'_1(x) = 6x(1-x)$ vanishes at 0 and 1. 4) They explain that offsetting each level by half the voxel size ($1/(2^{l+1})$ or $1/(2N_l)$) prevents zero derivatives from aligning across levels. 5) They state that this method is computationally efficient (hidden by memory bottlenecks) and that higher-order smoothsteps reduce reconstruction quality.
